title: Question 6
stem:
Fig. 6.1 shows a thin slice of semiconducting material used in a Hall probe.

{{figure:figure_6_1}}

Fig. 6.1 (not to scale)

Current $I$ passes through the slice in the direction shown.

The slice is placed in a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$, so that two of its faces are perpendicular to the magnetic field.

A steady Hall voltage $V_{\text{H}}$ is developed between face PQXW and face SRYZ.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Use the letters in Fig. 6.1 to identify the faces that are perpendicular to the magnetic field.
hints: Hint 1: Picture the three directions that must all be at right angles in a Hall probe - the current direction, the direction across which $V_H$ is measured, and the magnetic field direction. Which pair of faces is at right angles to both of the first two?
parts.proper_answer: The faces perpendicular to the magnetic field are PQRS and WXYZ.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Visualise the three perpendicular directions**
You are sitting with the slice in front of you. Current $I$ flows roughly from the R end to the W end, along the length of the slice. The Hall voltage $V_H$ is measured sideways, between face PQXW on one side and face SRYZ on the other side.

Step 2: **Find the third perpendicular direction**
In the Hall effect, magnetic field, current and Hall voltage directions are all mutually perpendicular. The only direction perpendicular to both the length (current) and the sideways direction is the vertical direction, top to bottom. So $B$ must enter through the top face and leave through the bottom face. Those are faces $PQRS$ and $WXYZ$.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Explain how the steady Hall voltage $V_{\text{H}}$ is developed between faces PQXW and SRYZ.

markscheme_points.text: force on charge carriers is perpendicular to both (magnetic) field and current
as charge carriers are deflected to one side, an electric field is set up
(steady V_H when) electric and magnetic forces on charge carriers are equal (and opposite)

hints: Hint 1: Start with what a single moving charge in the current feels when it moves across a magnetic field - in which direction does the magnetic force push it relative to its motion and to $B$?
Hint 2: Think about what happens if all the moving charges keep getting pushed to the same side face - how does one face become charged differently from the opposite face?
Hint 3: Consider what this build-up of charge itself creates between the two side faces, and when the build-up will stop growing to give a steady $V_H$.
parts.proper_answer: Moving charge carriers experience a magnetic force perpendicular to current and $B$ and are deflected to one side face. Charge separation sets up a transverse electric field and Hall voltage between PQXW and SRYZ. Steady $V_H$ is reached when electric force on carriers equals and opposes the magnetic force, so no further net deflection.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Magnetic deflection of the carriers**
Current is a flow of charge carriers with drift velocity $v$ along the slice. Because they move perpendicular to $B$, each feels a magnetic force $$F_B = Bqv$$ This force is perpendicular to both $v$ (the current direction) and $B$, by Fleming's left-hand rule. So carriers are pushed sideways toward either face PQXW or face SRYZ.

Step 2: **Charge build-up creates an electric field**
Carriers cannot leave the slice, so they pile up on one side face, leaving a deficit of charge (opposite sign) on the other side face. This separation of charge sets up an electric field $E_H$ across the width of the slice, from one Hall face to the other. The potential difference associated with this field is the Hall voltage $V_H$.

Step 3: **Steady state when forces balance**
As more charge builds up, the electric force $F_E = qE_H$ on a moving carrier grows and opposes the magnetic deflection. Very quickly equilibrium is reached where $$qE_H = Bqv$$ Then there is no further net sideways deflection and the charge separation and $V_H$ stay constant. That is the steady Hall voltage.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.part_stem: The magnitude of $V_{\text{H}}$ is given by the equation $$V_{\text{H}} = \frac{BI}{ntq}.$$
parts.text: State the meaning of the symbols $n$, $t$ and $q$. You may refer to the letters in Fig. 6.1.

markscheme_points.text: n: number density of charge carriers
t: distance PW (or SZ or QX or RY)
q: charge on each charge carrier

hints: Hint 1: Look at the denominator $ntq$ in $V_H = BI/ntq$ - one symbol must count how crowded the carriers are in the material, not how many in total.
Hint 2: Think about which dimension of the slice in Fig. 6.1 lies along the magnetic field direction you found in (a)(i) - the distance between those two faces.
Hint 3: Recall that current can be carried by electrons or holes, so the last symbol must describe the electrical property of a single moving particle.
parts.proper_answer: $n$ is the number density of charge carriers (number per unit volume). $t$ is the thickness of the slice parallel to $B$, i.e. distance PW (or SZ, QX, RY) between faces PQRS and WXYZ. $q$ is the charge on each charge carrier.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What $n$ means**
$n$ is not total number. It is number per unit volume: $$n = \frac{\text{number of free charge carriers}}{\text{volume}}$$ with unit $\text{m}^{-3}$. Semiconductors used for Hall probes have small $n$, which helps give a larger $V_H$.

Step 2: **What $t$ means**
$t$ is the dimension of the slice along $B$. Since $B$ is perpendicular to faces PQRS and WXYZ, $t$ is the separation between those faces. From the labels that is the short vertical edge, e.g. $$t = PW = SZ = QX = RY$$ This is the thickness of the thin slice.

Step 3: **What $q$ means**
$q$ is simply the charge carried by one charge carrier that contributes to current, e.g. $-e$ for electrons or $+e$ for holes, in coulombs. It appears because both the magnetic force $Bqv$ and the current $I = nAvq$ depend on the charge per carrier.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.text: Suggest, with reference to the equation, why the slice of the material used in a Hall probe is thin.

markscheme_points.text: (so t needs to be small for) V_H to be large enough to measure

hints: Hint 1: Rearrange your eye to see where $t$ sits in $V_H = BI/ntq$ - is it on top or bottom of the fraction, and what does that say about how $V_H$ changes if $t$ grows?
Hint 2: Think practically - for a given small $B$ you want to measure, would you prefer a tiny microvolt signal lost in noise or a larger, easily measured voltage?
parts.proper_answer: $V_H$ is inversely proportional to $t$, $V_H \propto 1/t$. A thin slice with small $t$ gives a larger $V_H$ for given $B$ and $I$, large enough to measure accurately.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Read the proportionality**
Keeping $B$, $I$, $n$ and $q$ constant, the equation $$V_H = \frac{BI}{ntq}$$ shows $$V_H \propto \frac{1}{t}$$ So halving the thickness doubles the Hall voltage. $t$ is in the denominator.

Step 2: **Why thin is better**
Hall voltages are often very small, especially for small $B$. Making $t$ very small boosts $V_H$ to a value that a voltmeter can measure reliably with good sensitivity. That is why a Hall probe uses a thin slice, and also a semiconductor with small $n$.
